nytimes.com.title: Unrest Mars Day of Protest in France, as Student Movement Turns National
nytimes.com.text:
Unrest flared across France on Saturday amid demonstrations against rising living and fuel costs that built on weeks of high school protests, heightening a sense of fiscal and social crisis in the country.
More than half a million people joined 110 marches throughout the country, according to the interior ministry, making it the biggest day of protest since unrest began to surge nationally roughly a month ago. One of France’s main unions, the C.G.T., estimated a higher number of 800,000 protesters.
The protests marked a convergence between a student-focused movement that has spurred demonstrations out of hundreds of schools, and a broader social movement that appeals to French citizens of different ages.
In many places, the protests were overtaken by violent confrontations between rioters and police officers, including in Marseille, France’s second-largest city, where people briefly broke into the city hall and knocked over a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the French Republic, before the police cleared them out. By nightfall, roughly 400 people, most of them adults, had been arrested across the country, according to the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez.

nytimes.com.title: Singing, Dancing and Getting Dumped by A.I. on Korean TV
nytimes.com.text:
He went on a pool date with an A.I. avatar, slept next to another and was dumped by a third.
These were scenes involving Kian84, a participant on “My A.I. Partner: Strange Love,” a South Korean reality TV show in which three celebrities explored whether they could have a romantic relationship with avatars powered by artificial intelligence.
The mechanics bordered on the absurd — the physical manifestation of the A.I. was a personality on a tablet. One of the avatars had a glitch during a karaoke outing: She would not stop singing, and eventually, the screen went blank.
“She was hurting,” her date, Kian84, a cartoonist whose real name is Kim Hee-min, said later on the show. “I felt a strange sense of pity,” he added, pointing to his heart.
In another episode, Mr. Kim was abandoned halfway though a fishing excursion by a different avatar, which concluded that they had nothing to talk about.
Airing on the SBS network and streaming on Netflix, the six-episode show concluded last month and was a modest ratings success. It provided a window into two dominant facets of life in South Korea today: loneliness and the country’s enthusiastic embrace of A.I.
Millions of South Koreans live alone, and the country’s traditional family-centered support system is unraveling. A.I. has helped fill some of that void — chatbots check in on seniors, and some cities use the technology in counseling isolated teenagers.

nytimes.com.title: In India, the Scion of a Political Dynasty Tries to Seize His Moment
nytimes.com.text:
Joining Gen Z protesters and confronting the police are not what one might expect of the middle-aged scion of India’s most illustrious political dynasty. But for Rahul Gandhi, they could be the opportunity of a lifetime.
For years, Mr. Gandhi has struggled to find his footing in the treacherously shifting sands of Indian politics. Even as head of the largest opposition party, he has had difficulty being seen as more than just the great-grandson of India’s first prime minister and the grandson and son of two others.
At 56, he may have found his moment by rising to oppose the strongman-style politics of the current prime minister, Narendra Modi, and stand with the youth movement that has taken to the streets against what its leaders see as a threat to the world’s largest democracy.
Mr. Gandhi has long warned Indians that their rights were being dismantled. His message caught fire over the summer, after leaks of questions for a college-entrance exam resulted in its cancellation, igniting massive student protests that led to the resignation of India’s education minister. Weeks later Mr. Gandhi claimed further vindication after the deletion of 130 million names from registration records again fueled national outrage and demands for the removal of India’s chief election commissioner.
Neerja Chowdhury, an author and political commentator, said people are more receptive to his message because “dissatisfaction with the government is growing, there’s fatigue, there’s no new energy,” on top of which Mr. Modi tends to come down with a heavy hand.

nytimes.com.title: Israeli Settlers Attack Palestinians and European Officials in West Bank
nytimes.com.text:
Masked Israeli settlers carried out an attack in a Palestinian town where residents and European diplomats were participating in the olive harvest on Saturday, a day after a similar assault injured several Palestinians and a U.S. journalist in the occupied West Bank.
The episode took place in Taybeh, a Christian town north of Jerusalem, when Palestinians were gathering olives alongside French, Polish and Belgian diplomats who were in attendance to show solidarity, Palestinian residents, local officials and witnesses said.
The extremists beat a Palestinian teenager, pushed an older woman and smashed the window of a Belgian diplomatic vehicle, said Suleiman Khourieh, the mayor of Taybeh. They also scuffled with the visiting mayor of a French town that had recently become a “sister city” of Taybeh, he said.
“This violence shows nobody is protected — not Palestinians, not journalists and not diplomats,” Mr. Khourieh said.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said in a statement that Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in the country’s north, was “violently assaulted by extremist settlers in the West Bank.” He called on Israel to “put an end to this criminal violence.”
On Friday, Israeli settlers beat a group of Palestinians and Heidi Levine, a longtime photographer for the Washington Post, with bats and sticks. Ms. Levine, 63, was in moderate condition after undergoing surgery on Saturday, according to Beilinson Hospital in central Israel. She suffered a broken rib and lacerations on her legs, rear end and hip, as well as a serious cut on her left hand, according to her family.

nytimes.com.title: Dispute Between Trump Allies Centers on Millions Transferred From Congo
nytimes.com.text:
The White House investigation into a dispute between two prominent Trump supporters, Richard Grenell and Alina Habba Mildon, centers on a bank transfer from the Democratic Republic of Congo to a Texas defense company, people familiar with the matter said.
Mrs. Mildon, a former personal lawyer for President Trump, stormed into the Oval Office last week accusing Mr. Grenell of siphoning millions of dollars from a business transaction in 2025 organized by a Turkish investor who later became her husband. Part of the money, she claimed, was meant to be set aside for a donation to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts but was never delivered to the institution. Mr. Grenell ran the Kennedy Center at the time.
Responding to questions from The New York Times, Mr. Grenell denied all accusations, calling them absurd. Mr. and Mrs. Mildon didn’t respond to requests for comment. The White House also did not respond.
The dispute and resulting investigation have unfolded at a time of internal turmoil for the Trump administration, with the dramatic exit of his new press secretary and officials with ties to the president.
Mrs. Mildon and Mr. Grenell had once been close friends but have fallen out in recent months over Mr. Mildon’s business dealings. Their feud became public in recent days, after The Times began to inquire about Mr. Mildon’s business activities and his contributions to the Kennedy Center. The questions prompted Mrs. Mildon to relay her accusations directly to Mr. Trump last Friday.
Mrs. Mildon initially told White House officials that the money, $17.6 million, came from her now-husband, Turhan Mildon, whom she married last month. The initial set of documents that her husband’s lawyer submitted to the White House, however, redacted the name of the sender, according to the people familiar with the matter.

nytimes.com.title: Kenya Confirms Four New Ebola Cases
nytimes.com.text:
Kenya confirmed four new cases of Ebola on Saturday, as the country’s Health Ministry sought to assuage fears that the virus could spread among the public at large.
The new infections, which bring the total in Kenya to seven, come days after the country announced its first-ever Ebola case on Oct. 6. A relative of the first patient and three health workers who treated him are among those infected, the Health Ministry said.
A disastrous Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, now the second largest on record, has killed more than 4,400 people there and infected more than twice that. The first case in Kenya, found in a man who died after arriving from Congo, raised worries of cross-border transmission.
Kenya’s border and Bunia, Congo, the city most deeply affected by the outbreak, are less than 500 miles apart, separated only by Uganda.
But Kenyan officials are saying that the virus is under control.
The Health Ministry said it had traced and quarantined most people who could be at risk of infection. “There is no evidence of community transmission of the disease,” the ministry said in a statement on Saturday.
The second and third Ebola patients, who are relatives of the first patient, are in stable condition and responding to treatment, the ministry added.
All of the cases in Kenya involve the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or accepted treatment, according to the World Health Organization.
While less deadly than the Zaire strain of the virus — which accounts for the majority of Ebola deaths in previous outbreaks — the Bundibugyo’s fatality rate can reach 50 percent, according to the United Nations.
The Congo outbreak, first discovered in the eastern region of Ituri, has become the largest in the country’s history. There have been more than 9,200 confirmed Ebola cases so far, according to government data.
Uganda has also recorded 20 cases and three deaths, largely among people arriving from Congo, the Ugandan authorities said, but the virus there was quickly contained, and the World Health Organization declared the Ugandan outbreak over in August.
Ebola controls have become contentious in Kenya, particularly after accusations that President William Ruto had bowed to U.S. interests by allowing the construction of an Ebola quarantine facility for Americans at an air base in central Kenya. Hundreds marched in June to protest that facility.

cnn.com.title: Trump and Netanyahu’s once blossoming bromance sours at a pivotal moment for both men
cnn.com.text: For years, Israelis driving the country’s highways in the final weeks of an election have seen the same image: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu standing beside President Donald Trump, under the slogan, “A different league.” Less than two weeks before the October 27 vote, the billboards of Netanyahu are back. This time, Trump is not on them. The president still appears in some videos for Netanyahu’s Likud party, but his absence may signal something beyond advertising. Trump has so far declined to endorse Netanyahu and has sidestepped questions on whether he should be reelected. “I’m not involved in [Israeli] politics anymore,” he told Time earlier this month. On Thursday, Trump told Newsmax Netanyahu would like him to be involved in the election. “I’ve had a very good relationship with him,” he said, but avoided endorsing him again. When asked directly whether he trusts Netanyahu, he said bluntly, “I don’t trust anybody in the world of politics.” For a campaign that has traditionally treated Netanyahu’s intimacy with the White House as a major electoral asset, the restraint is notable. Trump has starred in Netanyahu’s campaigns since 2013, when still a businessman and TV personality, he released a video urging Israelis to “vote for Benjamin.” When Trump entered the White House in 2017, he showered Netanyahu with political gifts. About two weeks before Israel’s April 2019 election, Netanyahu was in Washington to watch Trump sign a historic proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights. In January 2020, five weeks before Israelis went again to the polls, Trump unveiled the Israeli-Palestinian “Deal of the Century” plan. Netanyahu stood smiling by his side. Ahead of this election, there has been no red carpet. The last time Netanyahu and Trump met at the White House in August, there were no cameras. The two did not meet at all when Netanyahu traveled to New York for the UN General Assembly in September. Over the course of the last year, Netanyahu has taken steps that have drawn fury from Trump, including undermining Trump-led peace efforts by striking inside Lebanon and Gaza. Trump has cursed the prime minister out in phone calls and warned him he’s losing support among Americans, according to people familiar with the conversations. He’s asked why Israel was blowing up apartment buildings in Lebanon and warned about the risk of a global economic downturn as a result of the Iran war. Inside the White House, many of the moves were interpreted as election-year posturing by Netanyahu, whose internal politics are well known by Trump and his advisers. Over the summer, many Trump advisers came to the conclusion that Netanyahu was trying to prolong the Iran war to bolster his own political standing. Trump has given Netanyahu a degree of leeway because of those political concerns, people familiar with the matter said. But he’s still grown frustrated at some of Israel’s actions, many of which he believes run counter to American interests. Another person close to Trump suggested his lack of endorsement is tied to Netanyahu’s weakness in the polls. Trump has long been careful to avoid endorsing candidates who seem likely to lose. In conversations over the past several months, Trump has quizzed Netanyahu about the election and his prospects, according to people familiar with the matter. While Netanyahu has sought to project confidence, Trump is well aware of the prime minister’s difficult political position. As Netanyahu’s standing fell in the Trump administration, so did Trump’s standing in Israel. According to Israeli sources close to Netanyahu, Trump was originally meant to be a centerpiece of Netanyahu’s campaign. Last December, at Mar-a-Lago, the prime minister announced that Trump would become the first non-Israeli to receive the prestigious Israel Prize. Netanyahu aides hoped Trump would accept the prize in person at Israel’s Independence Day ceremony in April, giving jumpstarting the campaign. Then came the war with Iran. The joint US-Israeli attack began on February 28 with the two leaders projecting strategic harmony. Netanyahu thanked “my friend, President Donald Trump,” calling him “a leader who stands by his word.” Trump described the two of them as “war heroes” and publicly demanded that Israel’s president grant Netanyahu a pardon in his ongoing corruption trials. But Trump never showed interest in attending the Israel Prize ceremony. By then, the fighting in Iran had ended and ceasefire talks were underway. The Iran ceasefire and subsequent memorandum of understanding were deeply unpopular in Israel, particularly on the right. Yinon Magal, a pro-Netanyahu TV anchor, called Trump a “loser” after the deal was signed. A July survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute found that only 7% of Israelis had “a great deal of trust” that Trump “will do the right thing” on US-Israel relations, and 45% had none. “Trump’s stock in Israel, especially among right wing-voters, has weakened,” a Likud source said. “An endorsement would not necessarily have helped Netanyahu so much, so he did not invest much in it.” Another Likud source said, “It’s not as if Trump will endorse any other opponent, so it’s nice to have, but not a must.” Netanyahu’s opponents are watching, but with less alarm than before. “A year ago, our camp was calling anyone close to Trump to prevent an endorsement,” one senior opposition figure said. “Now it doesn’t really matter, the charm is not there.” Another opposition source said they had conveyed messages urging the White House to stay out of the race and appreciated that Trump has so far done so. When Trump was asked specifically about who is currently polling as Netanyahu’s leading challenger, he said, “Well, I don’t know, I don’t hear bad things about him.” He then said, “They’ve written Bibi off many, many times, just like they’ve written me off many, many times. I wouldn’t underestimate Bibi.” Trump has his own reasons for distance. American public opinion of Israel has fallen sharply, declining even more against the backdrop of the Iran war. Israel’s average net favorability fell from +51 points in July 2018 to -16 in July 2026, according to multiple polls, a 67-point drop over eight years. As America quickly soured on the Iran war, a source familiar with the relationship said, Trump has been “trying to shed the image that Netanyahu pulled him into it.” Still, the apparent distance may be misleading. Israeli sources say the two leaders have recently discussed renewed strikes on Iran. Israeli security sources told CNN preparations are underway - pending Trump’s decision - with timing unclear because of the US midterm elections. Netanyahu rejected suggestions he was seeking escalation before the vote. “It is not convenient for us, it’s no good,” he told Army Radio this week. He complained that if Iran fired missiles at Israel, his opponents “will blame me.”

cnn.com.title: ‘These are really tough times’: House Republicans confront voter fury over Trump’s Washington in final midterm stretch
cnn.com.text: GOP operatives conducting a focus group in a traditionally red Midwestern state this month were taken aback by what they heard from their own party’s voters. Asked what they blamed for rising gas prices, those voters pointed to “corrupt politicians” and “billionaires” — a response that surprised some longtime strategists who’ve never seen government corruption emerge as a top issue for so many Republican voters in congressional races, according to a person involved in the discussions. Those observations in the reliably red farm belt are just one instance of a glaring pattern for Republicans, as their House battlefield expands into places like Kentucky, Wisconsin and Arkansas. Even some GOP lawmakers acknowledge their party needs to do a better job of making sure they’re responding to voters’ anger at what they see as a broken system of government — or risk losing them altogether. “These are really tough times … Between their mortgage and their electric bill and the cost of everything else, they’re having a hard time making it. That’s real. That’s a lot more important than the other insider crap we deal with,” said GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew of New Jersey, who’s built a brand in Congress as a Trump-loving populist who’s willing to point out his own party’s failures on issues like rising healthcare costs. And while many voters blame politicians on both sides of the aisle, some Republicans fear they could soon take out those frustrations on the ones in charge. Republicans involved in House races from Texas to New York to Florida have privately acknowledged to CNN they’re troubled by flashes of anger particularly from working-class voters with kids, whose gas and grocery prices are skyrocketing. One GOP consultant working on congressional races described the theme of corruption as an “underappreciated fact” of this midterm, calling it a “two or three issue” in polling even in reliably red seats this cycle. There are fears that Republicans could see a washout in parts of the country that are suffering the most from high fuel and grocery prices — where they worry many blue-collar workers are feeling ignored by the president who once pledged to drain the swamp and, instead, has made plans to build a ballroom in it with a price tag in the millions. Republicans are mostly downbeat about holding onto the House, though they believe the Senate is still in reach, given that Democrats would likely need to win red states like Iowa, Alaska or Ohio. Even so, inside the GOP, multiple House Republican operatives say they are seeing some slight glimmers of optimism as internal polling in some races has improved from what many saw as a doomsday scenario a few weeks ago. Several believe they’re seeing evidence that some voters are coming “home,” especially in races with strong candidates, and that the hundreds of millions of dollars being poured into those contests may be starting to help. “In some places the polls are moving in our direction,” one GOP operative involved in House races told CNN, declining to offer specifics because of the competitive nature of the campaigns. But the House map is still not a rosy picture for the party, whose president is underwater in states he won by double digits two years ago. Top GOP super PACs have cut off funding for two incumbents so far, which CNN first reported was under consideration, as well as several seats they were attempting to flip. Top Democrats, for their part, remain confident they will win the majority – and not by a small margin. They feel particularly good about defeating incumbent GOP Reps. Monica De La Cruz of Texas, Juan Ciscomani in Arizona, Gabe Evans in Colorado plus Ryan Mackenzie and Scott Perry in Pennsylvania. That’s on top of the two incumbents already abandoned by GOP groups, according to multiple people familiar with internal polling. They’re also confident they’ll win in the open seat in North Carolina’s 11th , where GOP leaders pressured Rep. Chuck Edwards not to seek reelection, and Nebraska’s 2nd, where Republicans also pulled resources. Republicans are still spending in most of these races and say their own internal polling shows a path to victory, particularly for Ciscomani and Evans and possibly De La Cruz. There’s also hope of last-minute enthusiasm boost in seats like North Carolina’s 11th, where Vice President JD Vance is scheduled to visit early this week. One GOP operative involved in House races described each of those Democratic targets as “pure tossups.” There is some nervousness within the GOP conference about incumbents like Rep. French Hill in Arkansas and Brad Finstad in Minnesota who are in deep red seats, though few actually believe they will flip. They anticipate seats like those will be closer, and more expensive, than people in the party want — but most do not expect the worst. One Republican operative, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity, stressed that he does not believe an incumbent like Hill is at risk of losing: “If French Hill’s losing, it’s a f**king bloodbath. I don’t see it.” While Republicans have rolled their eyes at some of Democrats’ most ambitious targets, the party has increasingly put real money behind expanding the map. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, is leading a $20 million effort to push into red territory, including by trying to flip French’s seat. In an interview, Pritzker said he was trying to divert GOP money from more traditional battleground races and “support candidates where it might be a Trump +10 (district), but honestly, our candidate is running even or even ahead.” Trump hasn’t ruled out keeping the House, telling Van Drew in a phone call last week: “We still have a shot,” the lawmaker recalled. And Speaker Mike Johnson has said that the environment “feels like 2024” - when Trump won and Republicans kept the House and flipped the Senate. Johnson also said he believed polling may be underestimating GOP voter enthusiasm. “I am there on the ground in the swing districts that are going to decide the majority, and I am telling you something is happening right now,” Johnson said as part of a frenzied multi-state swing from Maine to Texas. “I’m telling you, the polling is not reflecting this.” Not every Republican shares that level of optimism. “This is a really bad time right now … Just how bad, we don’t know yet,” Van Drew added, though he predicted that Republicans could still avoid a blue wave. GOP operatives add that the Democratic Party’s brand, too, remains unpopular with voters and several of their incumbents have been swamped by corruption attack ads on TV. (Republicans have gone after Reps. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, Vicente Gonzalez of Texas and Adam Gray of California in particular.) Scores of Democratic candidates across the country have also found the issue effective against Republicans. Sam Forstag, a first-time candidate and labor leader, has run an insurgent populist campaign in Montana’s 1st district that’s forced Republicans to spend time and money defending the open seat. “Corruption, like a lot of other things in last couple years, is something that used to be spoken about in polite terms and hushed terms and now it’s all out in the open,” Forstag told CNN. He argued that Trump won the presidency twice by talking about this same issue – but then failed to deliver. “Trump told everybody one singular truth. He said the system is broken … While he was saying that, well, we had a Democrat in the White House telling us the economy is better than we think it is,” Forstag said, referring to then-President Joe Biden. “One of those two messages was a lot, had a lot more veracity to it than the other, and unfortunately, it turned out that [Trump] was lying about all the ways they were going to fix these things.”

cnn.com.title: Deadly fire breaks out after ‘serious incident’ at Canada military base
cnn.com.text: A major fire caused deaths and injuries at one of Canada’s busiest military bases on Saturday, sparked by an unspecified “serious incident.” The fire began at the base in Wainwright, a town in eastern Alberta province, according to officials, and “spread rapidly due to high winds,” said the municipal district in a Facebook post Saturday evening. A call for assistance came around 4 p.m., according to the Wainwright Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Defense Minister David McGuinty said in a video statement “that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base.” He did not provide details about the number of casualties or what caused the initial blaze, but called it an “active and delicate situation” and said an investigation would be launched soon. Late Saturday night, the municipal district said the fire was “being held at this time,” though fire crews will continue to monitor the area. CFB Wainwright, located about 210 kilometers (130 miles) southeast of provincial capital Edmonton, is one of the country’s busiest Army bases, according to a government website. It houses the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre. It’s also a training ground for Army field force units based in Edmonton. Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the fire had stemmed from “a serious incident,” without specifying details. A code orange, which designates an emergency response protocol for a high number of patients, has been declared in Edmonton, according to CNN’s newsgathering partner CBC, citing emergency department physician Dr. Warren Thirsk at the city’s Royal Alexandra Hospital. “It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster,” he said, adding that Wainwright’s healthcare centers have been “completely overwhelmed.” Patients are now being diverted to hospitals across Edmonton. CNN has reached out to the Royal Alexandra Hospital, other Edmonton health centers, and Alberta Health Services for comment. CNN has also reached out to the military base, the Wainwright fire department, the Alberta premier’s office, and the municipal district. The Canadian Armed Forces, the federal government, provincial and local authorities are cooperating “to mobilize all necessary support, and working through the details of what actually occurred,” McGuinty said. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith called the disaster “significant and tragic,” saying it was “affecting many of our brave military personnel.” No evacuation order has been issued. Authorities have asked residents to avoid the incident area, keep roads clear, and avoid visiting the Wainwright Health Center except for critical medical needs. “I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister … I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” McGuinty said in the video statement, responding to a journalist’s question. Opposition leader Pierre Poilievre also wrote in a post that he had spoken to McGuinty and Carney about the fire, thanked emergency responders, and added: “Pray for Wainwright, everyone.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

cnn.com.title: Abdul El-Sayed disavows Muslim Brotherhood and criticizes implications that he has ‘dual loyalty’
cnn.com.text: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Saturday disavowed the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist political movement, during a heated exchange at a town hall. El-Sayed, who could make history as the first Muslim elected to the Senate, has frequently faced Republican accusations that he is sympathetic to interests connected to Islamic terror. In recent days, Republicans including his GOP challenger, Mike Rogers, and President Donald Trump have commented about potential connections to the organization. An attendee at a town hall in Caro, Michigan, repeatedly pressed El-Sayed about the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he had yet to hear the candidate reject the organization. “Abdul, will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?” the man shouted from the crowd. El-Sayed, after disavowing the movement, blasted the man for implicitly assuming his “dual loyalty.” “You assume … that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution,” El-Sayed said. He later added, “For me, that Constitution is the guiding light.” The audience member walked out after the exchange as the crowd cheered for El-Sayed. The nominee has faced questions about potential connections to the organization. The latest attacks came after old tweets from El-Sayed’s half-sister resurfaced online, including a post from 2012 in which she described having “an amazing talk with my mom about her activism in the Muslim Brotherhood during the early 70s while she was in college.” Earlier this week, El-Sayed denied allegations that he or his family has ties with the Muslim Brotherhood, telling reporters that to think that anybody in his family was part of the organization was “an insane thing to assume.” El-Sayed has said he does not know what his mother was doing in Egypt during the 1970s, explaining he was 3 when his parents divorced and didn’t see his mother for years after being raised by his father and stepmother. “They want to talk about me or point to my mom or my sister,” El-Sayed said on Thursday, adding, “I’m running for office. Judge me by my actions and my work.” The Muslim Brotherhood is an Islamist movement with global offshoots that once wielded significant political power in Egypt, where it was founded. The movement officially rejects the use of violent means to secure its goals. However, offshoots of the group have been linked to attacks in the past. Trump signed an executive order in November that initiated a process by which certain chapters or other subdivisions of the Muslim Brotherhood could be considered for designation as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. El-Sayed has suggested that questions about supposed ties to the Muslim Brotherhood are rooted in bigotry. “To insinuate that somehow, because of my Muslim faith, as somebody who might be the first senator who has that faith, that I would have anything but allegiance to the Constitution, that should be called into question,” El-Sayed said Sunday on MSNOW.

cnn.com.title: Mexico arrests state official accused of allowing unauthorized CIA role in drug raid
cnn.com.text: Months after a deadly car wreck revealed the CIA’s participation in a raid on a Chihuahua drug lab, authorities arrested César Jáuregui, Chihuahua’s former attorney general, for allegedly allowing US spies to participate in the operation without permission from the Mexican government. Gilberto Loya Chávez, the acting head of the Chihuahua Attorney General’s Office, said in a video message that Jáuregui is under investigation for unlawful exercise of public service and conspiracy by public officials. Jáuregui is due to appear before a judge, Loya Chávez added, but did not say when. The arrest, the official explained, came after the Attorney General’s Office concluded that there had been misconduct in an April operation in which state officials dismantled a clandestine drug-manufacturing laboratory. The CIA’s participation came to light soon after the raid on April 19. That day, while he was still attorney general, Jáuregui himself announced that four people had died in a car crash as they were returning from a drug raid in northern Chihuahua: two Mexican law enforcement officials and two Americans, whom he identified as instructors from the US Embassy in Mexico City. Days later, CNN and other media outlets revealed that the two Americans were not just embassy workers: they were CIA agents. The agency has significantly expanded its clandestine anti-cartel operations in the country during President Donald Trump’s second term – including assassinations of alleged cartel members and drone flights over Mexican territory. On Saturday, Loya Chávez was careful to say that the issue at hand was not the drug raid itself, but rather the participation of US officials outside the bounds of Mexican law. “This action does not disregard the work of the State Investigation Agency, the State Attorney General’s Office, or the Armed Forces in dismantling the clandestine laboratory, because it is of course a very significant result in the fight against organized crime,” Loya Chávez said. “What is being investigated is the way this operation was conducted, the failure to observe the chain of command and the applicable protocols.” “A good result does not justify breaking the law,” the official added. CNN has contacted Jáuregui’s office to find out whether he already has legal representation and whether he has entered a plea. The presence of CIA agents in the operation incensed the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum, which took Chihuahua authorities to task for failing to give prior notice and coordinate with their federal counterparts, as required by Mexican law. Sheinbaum has insisted ever since that the situation had to be investigated to determine whether any crime had been committed. The president said at the time that her office had been unaware that state officials in Chihuahua and the US government were collaborating independently. “The relationship is federal, not state,” Sheinbaum said. “They must have authorization from the federal government for this collaboration, which necessarily takes place at the state level, as established by the Constitution.” Soon after, Chihuahua Governor María Eugenia Campos ordered the creation of a unit to investigate the case. On April 27, in her first report on the matter, special prosecutor Wendy Chávez said there were indications that the director of Chihuahua’s state security agency, who died in the car crash, had “possible unofficial collaboration” with the US agents and did not inform his superiors that they would be taking part in the operation. Jáuregui resigned as attorney general that same day, stating that he was accepting “political responsibility” for the tensions the matter had generated. “There were omissions both in the information provided and in the institutional handling of the points of contact with these individuals,” he said. Until his arrest on Saturday, Jáuregui had been seeking the conservative National Action Party nomination for mayor of Chihuahua, the state’s capital.

cnn.com.title: Final plans for 250-foot triumphal arch omit Trump’s idea for military complex
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration on Friday released final plans for its proposed 250-foot triumphal arch, notably excluding key features of a military complex including drones and snipers that President Donald Trump used as justification for the controversial project. In the new documents, made public by the federal National Capital Planning Commission, the contours of the arch do not appear to reflect a national security purpose. Instead, the plans submitted describe the project as a “ceremonial gateway” to the nation’s capital. Trump announced in September that the arch that would sit directly across Arlington National Cemetery would store large numbers of drones and function as a post for military snipers, with a large cache of ammunition. The proposed arch is among several projects Trump is pursuing in an effort to remake the nation’s capital in his image, prompting legal battles from preservationists and others. The idea of the arch being needed for national security purposes mirrors an argument Trump has made for building a White House ballroom where the East Wing once stood. The proposed arch would sit squarely in a traffic circle connecting Washington DC to Virginia, with an observation deck offering views of Arlington National Cemetery. Veterans suing to stop its construction argue that the towering structure would break the solemnity of funerals at the cemetery, while preservations argue it would disrupt the sightline of the row of national landmarks that includes the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington House and the Robert E. Lee Memorial. While the plans submitted Friday don’t include the military components Trump described, the structure still might feature them. An Interior Department spokesperson told CNN on Saturday that the current design of the triumphal arch is capable of accommodating the national security functions Trump highlighted in a social media post. The agency spokesperson said the structure will “enhance the visitor experience at Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike.” The Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, a little-known independent federal agency within the executive branch, conducted a private call last week on the matter. The agency said that an analysis on the use of the arch as a military asset would be considered separately from construction plans that had already been making their way through a historical review and approval process, according to two sources close to the matter. An evaluation on the historical impact of using the arch as a military complex would have to come at the request of the Department of Defense, which has yet to submit a request to the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation. This dual track — approving the arch construction plans and the separate intent to use it as a military complex — sidesteps questions over whether the arch would need to be reviewed and approved by key commissions all over again. The Pentagon referred CNN to the White House for comment, who has not responded to CNN’s inquiry. The plans without the complex have been approved by the Commission of Fine Arts and have received preliminary approval from the National Capital Planning Commission, the two key federal agencies that oversee architecture and design changes in DC The National Capital Planning Commission has not given final go-ahead for the project but the administration is eyeing November’s meeting for approval.

cnn.com.title: Buildings torched and over 1,000 detained after half a million protesters sweep France
cnn.com.text: Riots broke out across major French cities on Saturday night as unrest spread beyond the capital, with government buildings torched and more than 1,000 people detained by police. In the central city of Limoges, the historic town hall was set ablaze, with video showing its roof collapsing. In Marseille, black-clad protesters broke into city hall and defaced the building, and in Lyon, protesters torched the city’s tourist office, the Reuters news agency reported. As night fell in Paris, groups of young people looted and started fires as protests ended, prompting police to respond with tear gas and baton charges in the narrow streets. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 1,200 people had been detained nationwide in the unrest, and condemned the “unacceptable levels of violence.” The destruction followed what had been largely peaceful protests, which have grown out of sweeping student-led rallies that gripped parts of France last month, sparking a broader movement against crumbling schools, the spiking cost of living, and perceived government inaction. The rallies have become emblematic of long-simmering, intergenerational anger among people who say their calls for social and political change are going unmet by negligent governments. Some 550,000 protesters hit the streets across France, including 110,000 in Paris, interior minister Laurent Nunez said. Organizers estimated an even higher turnout. “There’s an accumulation of wealth and power that’s completely out of control,” one protester, who gave her name as Pauline, told CNN in Paris on Saturday. “We’re also here to support the youth. There are victories, but if we look at the bigger picture, it’s not going in the right direction,” the 36-year-old added. Another demonstrator complained of “less democracy” and a “concentration of power” under President Emmanuel Macron’s leadership. “There are billionaires who control the media,” Louise, 38, told CNN. “We are fighting to change things.” Macron slammed “sowers of chaos” for interfering with peaceful protests, and warned late on Saturday that “those who have broken, attacked (police) prefectures, as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished.” “We do not back down in the face of rioters and those who’ve come to attack law enforcement,” said the Paris Police Prefecture – the body that oversees the Paris Police Force, emergency services and various other administrative departments – adding that its staffers stood “their ground with courage and professionalism.” The police response to the weeks of protest has come under scrutiny. Earlier in the week, that response had left a 14-year-old boy with a fractured jaw. Another police officer was captured on camera using a headlock on a girl in the northwestern area of Alençon, an action now prohibited by law. A protester in the city of Saint-Étienne, about 40 miles southwest of Lyon, lost his hand during a march there on Saturday, a police source told CNN affiliate BFMTV. This is the second reported instance of a demonstrator losing their hand in the current wave of student protests. A student in the northeastern city of Lens lost his hand after reportedly picking up a grenade earlier this month, prompting the temporary suspension of one type of stun grenade by police. That ban, which still allowed police to use several different grenades, has now been rescinded. Overall, authorities said that the “vast majority of individuals” had demonstrated peacefully on Saturday, according to BFMTV. Posting on X, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left La France Insoumise Party, emphasized that the majority of demonstrators on Sunday had made their point peacefully. “While news channels are flooded with images of violence in dozens of cities, everything is unfolding peacefully with tens of thousands of people calmly mobilized. Two worlds, two realities.” Youth activists led solidarity protests in Belgium, Albania and Italy on Saturday as well. Earlier this fall, high school students in France organized scattered protests demanding reduced class sizes, increased spending on teachers, investments in infrastructure designed to withstand the climate crisis and end to police violence against young people. In the past decade and a half, a rise in fertility coupled with funding cuts has led to more students, but fewer teachers in classrooms. The French Education Minister Edouard Geffray has met with student protesters multiple times in recent weeks, although an agreement is yet to be made. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Israeli settlers attack group of European diplomats in the occupied West Bank
cnn.com.text: Israeli settlers attacked a group of European diplomats in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, one day after a Washington Post journalist was injured in another assault. Settlers attacked the group of European diplomats in the village of Taybeh, a Palestinian Christian village east of Ramallah, according to Israeli media and Wafa, the official Palestinian news agency. The diplomats, local media reported, were from France, Belgium and Poland. Belgium’s Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot slammed the attack and said it was a directly related to Israeli policies in the West Bank. “As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice,” he said in a statement on X. “Impunity for violent settlers must end.” He said the group also included Catholic representatives. Poland’s Foreign Ministry condemned the attack in a statement on social media, saying that they “expect the Israeli authorities to provide urgent and detailed explanations, identify those responsible and ensure that they are held accountable.” “We are deeply outraged by this incident and condemn it in the strongest possible terms,” the ministry said. “Poland has consistently opposed violence perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Attacks against members of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable.” French Foreign Minister Jean-Nöel Barrot called the attack “outrageous” in a social media post, urging the Israeli government to arrest those responsible immediately. In one video from the scene, a French official, identified as Aulnoye-Aymeries mayor Bernard Baudoux, is sitting on the ground outside a vehicle with a smashed window. In other videos, masked settlers – some armed with clubs or riding all-terrain vehicles – are blocking the roads and demanding identification. Hussein al-Sheikh, Vice President of the Palestinian Authority, called on the international community to hold Israel responsible for the attack. “This is a miniature model of the scale of the daily terrorism to which our Palestinian people are subjected, and it requires a firm international stance that imposes international protection for the Palestinian people.” Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said he strongly condemns “the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters.” He said the foreign ministry was in touch with the ambassadors of the countries involved and was assisting law enforcement. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said there were no soldiers in the area at the time of the attack, and the visit had not been coordinated with the military. “The IDF strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters,” the IDF said. Israeli police are investigating. The settler attack on the diplomats comes one day after a different incident in which settlers attacked veteran Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine as she accompanied a group of Palestinians for the start of the annual olive harvest. Levine was hospitalized and required surgery after the assault, during which she said her camera and passport were stolen. She said the assault lasted about 10 minutes, even though she was clearly wearing a protective vest that identified her as press. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has repeatedly downplayed settler violence, tried to cast doubt on the attack. He said that Israel “unequivocally condemns violence against anyone,” but he issued no condemnation of the masked and armed settlers who were seen on video attacking Levine. Despite clear and unequivocal condemnation from Sa’ar and Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who called the attack on diplomats “outrageous and shocking violence,” Netanyahu once again tried to question the veracity of Saturday’s settler violence, with his office saying in a statement on X that “SERIOUS ACCUSATIONS REQUIRE SERIOUS EVIDENCE.”

cnn.com.title: Trump administration seeks to remove judge in golf course case, accusing her of ‘egregious’ behavior
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration has requested the removal of the federal judge overseeing a legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s plans to overhaul a Washington, DC public golf course, accusing her of having “bias.” In a motion filed Friday, the administration’s lawyer said US District Judge Ana Reyes’ “behavior in this case is nothing short of egregious,” pointing to a tense hearing earlier this week. CNN previously reported that during Monday’s hearing, Reyes — who was appointed to the bench by former President Joe Biden — said she was “furious” with the Trump administration for cutting down 169 trees from the East Potomac Golf Course without first notifying the court, adding that “the government can’t be trusted.” In Friday’s filing, the Justice Department lawyer said, “Judge Reyes’s conduct rises to the level of deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy toward the Trump Administration,” raising comments she made when overseeing other cases involving the administration. “The Trump Administration is entitled to a neutral forum and an adjudicator who is capable of maintaining the appearance of impartiality,” the lawyer continued. “Judge Reyes has demonstrated she cannot do that.” Friday’s filing is part of a legal challenge from a preservationist group and two local golfers against Trump’s plans to transform the East Potomac Golf Course into a championship caliber course. The proposed renovation is among several construction projects that the president has launched since returning to the White House as part of his efforts to reshape Washington, DC’s physical landscape. Federal officials said in a recent court filing that nearly 730 trees will need to be cleared as part of the renovation plan, describing it as routine maintenance meant to eliminate potential hazards. The administration’s lawyer also took issue with Reyes requiring “high-level” officials to be at the Monday hearing, writing that she “demonstrates a cavalier disregard for these officials’ valuable time, as well as a blatant disregard for black-letter separation of powers principles she should be aware of as a federal judge.” The lawyer went on to point to comments that Reyes previously made when overseeing other cases involving the Trump administration to argue that there is a “pattern of animus.” According to the filing, Reyes said the administration is “literally erasing transgender people” with its ban on transgender service members. The judge ultimately blocked the ban.

cnn.com.title: It wouldn’t be easy to strip Rep. Ilhan Omar of her citizenship, legal experts say
cnn.com.text: The search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, home by federal law enforcement earlier this week was an extraordinary legal step taken against a sitting congresswoman who is facing reelection. The Justice Department pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Omar’s home while the congresswoman has said she believes the administration is ultimately seeking to intimidate her. The government has not yet indicated it will take steps to attempt to strip Omar of her citizenship. But the president himself has said he’d like to see Omar sent to Somalia. “Fake “Congresswoman” Illhan Omar, a constant complainer who hates the USA, knows everything there is to know. She should be in jail, or even a worse punishment, sent back to Somalia, considered one of the absolutely worst countries in the World,” President Donald Trump posted on Truth social earlier this year. “She could help to MAKE SOMALIA GREAT AGAIN!” Omar has not been charged with a crime, and the Justice Department has not revealed any evidence against her. But the path for the federal government to attempt denaturalization wouldn’t be an easy one, legal experts told CNN. Citizenship has long been considered “a kind of a safe harbor,” said Daniel Kanstroom, a Boston College professor who teaches immigration law. “It’s hard to get, but once you get it, the standard for the government to take it away is really, really high.” Challenges ahead Sources told CNN the search was related to an immigration-fraud probe investigating whether Omar’s father lied about her age when she obtained her citizenship in 2000. Omar maintains she was born in Somalia in 1982 and spent the first years of her life in that country as it was embroiled in a deadly civil war. She has said she came to the US around age 12, and about five years later, she became a US citizen. The federal investigators are looking at whether Omar lied about her age of 17 when she was applying for citizenship, and potentially whether that may have been a false statement repeated in recent years that could be prosecuted now. Denaturalization, the process of stripping a naturalized citizen of their citizenship, is an arduous and, until recently, relatively rare process typically reserved for extraordinary lies or omissions made during the naturalization process. It was used frequently to strip the US citizenships of former Nazis who lied about their wartime activities — the Department of Justice had a unit called the Office of Special Investigations that was formed specifically for this purpose — and has also been used against naturalized members of terrorist and other criminal organizations. Since Trump took office last year, the Justice Department has said it would prioritize some denaturalization proceedings, which take place as lawsuits filed against citizens in federal court. Between 2008 and June 12, 2026, 166 denaturalization complaints were filed, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an annual average of less than 10, and a miniscule fraction compared to the hundreds of thousands of people who became newly naturalized every year. But the second Trump administration has sought to ramp up those numbers as part of its efforts to curb and repeal nearly all forms of immigration — legal and illegal — into the United States. Earlier this month, the government announced it was moving to strip citizenship from 40 naturalized citizens through cases filed since August 21. Under recent previous administrations, civil denaturalization cases were relatively rare. Between 2008 and 2024, 116 civil denaturalization lawsuits were filed, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, an average of less than seven cases a year. But the second Trump administration has significantly ramped up those numbers as part of its efforts to curb immigration, filing more than 160 civil denaturalization cases this year alone as of September 28, according to TRAC’s analysis. “It’s a significant increase,” said Texas-based attorney Dan Gividen, a former Immigration and Customs Enforcement attorney during the Obama administration who is currently defending about 10 clients from denaturalization. “For the government to go forward on either a criminal or civil denaturalization back then, the person had to warrant that kind of attention,” Gividen said. The government could seek to denaturalize someone either through civil proceedings, or by obtaining a criminal conviction for naturalization fraud. There is no statute of limitations for civil denaturalization proceedings. The criminal offense, however, is generally subject to a 10-year window where it can be brought after a person becomes a citizen, so it would likely not be applicable in a case against Omar, who obtained her citizenship more than two decades ago. A case against Omar Omar has been under criminal investigations in recent years, including before Trump took office last year. The current federal investigation is looking at whether Omar could have committed immigration fraud, and repeated false statements when filling out government documents, such as a passport, in recent years, and that could be considered a continuation of any suspected fraud. Further detail of what prosecutors have gathered about Omar’s immigration and government records so far have been presented to a court confidentially and aren’t yet available to the public. However, more than a dozen media organizations and the right-leaning transparency advocacy group Judicial Watch asked a court this week to release more of investigators’ records that supported the search. While the judge will hear from the Justice Department next week about those transparency requests, the criminal investigation continues. Federal investigators gaining access to records found in Omar’s DC home is likely to progress slowly, as federal investigators could spend weeks or months trying to obtain some of the congresswoman’s documents. If Omar were ever to be charged with a crime related to alleged immigration fraud, the Justice Department would have to prove that any misleading statements in immigration documents were made intentionally. Process that could take years The question of a possible deportation or denaturalization for Omar would also likely loom far in the future, even if there was evidence found of an immigration fraud crime. Contested denaturalizations typically take between one to three years to process in district court, not including appeals, said Peter Loblack, an Orlando-based immigration attorney. Even if a person has their citizenship stripped, deportation is not an immediate given. A denaturalized citizen would revert to their most recent status — typically, a lawful permanent resident or green card holder — and then the government would have to seek to have them deported through an entirely different proceeding. That also means that someone who is denaturalized could, theoretically, be renaturalized at a later date and under a different administration. CNN’s Priscilla Alvarez and Catherine Shoichet contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: Why the Katie Zacharia debacle is a huge embarrassment for Trump and his White House
cnn.com.text: Katie Zacharia was on a media tour to save her job as White House press secretary on Friday when “Fox and Friends” host Lawrence Jones asked whether she wished she had disclosed never passing the bar exam, despite repeatedly claiming to be a lawyer. Zacharia’s response: “Those questions weren’t asked.” And therein lies the problem: It’s not a matter of qualifications — it’s a basic question about her background that President Donald Trump and his White House failed to vet. Zacharia’s stunningly short and turbulent tenure as press secretary is far from the biggest or most substantial foul-up of Trump’s second term. But it does rank remarkably high on the embarrassment quotient. In one fell swoop over the course of a week, the White House confirmed how rudderless, impulsive and hubristic its entire operation is — and with just a few weeks to go before voters render their judgment on it in the 2026 midterm elections. Trump fired Zacharia as press secretary on Friday, advisers told CNN, just five days after she started the job. Her tenure has set the new benchmark for brevity as a top Trump White House aide, halving the record set by first-term Trump communications director Anthony Scaramucci. (“A Scaramucci” has since become an informal unit measuring 11 days.) Given that Trump personally selected Zacharia and he is generally loath to admit he’s made a mistake, it took a pretty rough week to prompt her ouster. In her inaugural briefing on Tuesday, Zacharia spent most of a 14-minute appearance nervously reading from a script that she repeatedly stumbled over before calling on just three reporters from conservative-friendly outlets. Then she went on a stream of media appearances that only reinforced she would likely be a liability at the White House lectern. Trump subsequently pulled the plug without even giving her a second briefing. It’s embarrassing for a number of reasons. It’s not as if Zacharia was the product of a process that needed to be rushed; former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced her departure more than two months ago, on August 12. That’s plenty of time to make sure you have the right person. The White House did have a series of candidates, CNN has reported, but some of them suffered from the unforgivable deficit of having occasionally said negative things about Trump. Zacharia’s name emerged suddenly late in the process, after not being previously considered. And as with so many things, it appears those around Trump quickly turned his whim into reality. There are understandable reasons for why Trump might have thought she could do the job, of course. He had undoubtedly seen her defending him on cable news plenty of times, his preferred method for screening job candidates. But serving as press secretary isn’t the same as doing TV hits with often-friendly hosts. And her briefing performance was objectively brutal. Then the White House compounded its mess. It dispatched Zacharia on a media tour of friendly outlets, apparently in hopes of rallying support and showing she was up to the task. But it proved the opposite. She was peppered with tough questions from conservative Trump allies who were ostensibly worried about her ability to handle being the face of the White House’s messaging. And those appearances — more than the briefing — made Trump conclude that she “wasn’t ready for prime time,” a person with direct knowledge of his comments told CNN. One of those skeptical conservative Trump allies was Fox News’ Sean Hannity. On Tuesday night, he was reading from the typical playbook: bashing the “abusively biased, corrupt news media” for being mean to Zacharia. But during his interview with her Thursday night, he asked her a series of sober and probing questions. Trump on Friday bemoaned how Zacharia was “made to suffer like she’s suffered at the hands of the press.” But it’s a lot harder to make that argument when your own media allies have done the scrutinizing. (Some of them also dinged Zacharia for her resume inflation.) And similar to Hannity, the White House now has egg on its face after initially vouching for Zacharia. White House communications director Steven Cheung assured in an excitable social media post Tuesday morning that Zacharia had a “tremendous start” in which she “commanded the room.” A White House press release hailed her “commanding” performance and clipped what it cast as her highlights. Later in the week, Cheung insisted she would be remembered as “one of the all-time greats” by the end of Trump’s second term. Oops. But perhaps the worst part of this whole episode for the White House is that it further solidifies a pre-existing narrative of Trump’s chaotic leadership style and inability to effectively manage the federal government. There’s been plenty of grist for that mill, including Trump’s recently aborted decisions to run taxpayer-funded political ads and to live stream an execution — both of which 80%-plus Americans opposed. Earlier in his presidency, Trump rained chaos on the government by giving Elon Musk apparent carte blanche to do, seemingly, more or less whatever he wanted. Many people who were fired later had to be reinstated when it was discovered that, actually, they did really important jobs — or couldn’t legally be fired. There was Signalgate and the whiplash over Trump’s tariffs and the administration’s inability to get its story straight on the Iran war. Similar to Zacharia, Trump also removed officials shortly after the Senate confirmed them, including the head of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and his IRS commissioner. (In the latter case, he also removed the acting replacement after less than a week.) His first national security adviser was moved to another job after less than three months, thanks to Signalgate. And the American people appear to have noticed. A CNN poll in July showed they disapproved of Trump’s management of the federal government, 65%-35%. Fully 74% of independents and even 28% of Republicans and GOP-leaning independents disapproved. “A Zacharia” doesn’t have the same ring to it as “a Scaramucci” does. But her tenure is an unforced error that gives voters a similar shorthand at a remarkably inopportune time for Trump.

cnn.com.title: Abbey Graf has a bare-bones budget and a spending aversion. But an expert says she can spend more and still meet her goals
cnn.com.text: Abbey Graf readily describes herself as frugal. And after speaking with the 28-year-old for the first time and reviewing her financial situation, certified financial planner Stacy Francis couldn’t agree more. “Her budget is one of the most bare-bones budgets I’ve ever seen,” Stacy said. Abbey has two main savings goals: Possibly buy a house and retire comfortably – maybe even retire early. To those ends, she tries to keep a tight rein on her spending today and save aggressively. For example, Abbey cooks a lot at home, not just because she likes to but because it saves her money. She has avoided taking up many hobbies because she worries about the expenses involved. She also keeps her other living expenses – including her rent – to a minimum. She drives a 21-year-old car that she owns outright and is almost done paying down her remaining $2,000 in student loans, which is her only debt. Abbey’s challenge is not to save more – she’s already socking away a quarter of her $74,000 income. Rather, she needs to get a better sense of what her current savings can do for her. “I’d like a plan of what I would need for retirement. I’m not sure what the goal post is,” Abbey said. Her other big challenge is finding ways to alleviate her financial anxieties about whether she has enough to secure her future. Stacy is creating a financial plan with a few different scenarios to give Abbey a concrete sense of how “on track” she is to meet her goals of buying a house within a few years and retiring comfortably (even if she retires early). Given Abbey’s anxieties about spending money and fear of not having enough, Stacy plans to use very conservative assumptions for inflation, health costs and average returns when making her projections based on Abbey’s savings today. “I’d also like a scenario where she spends more money. I’d love for her to do some travel and enjoy her 20s,” Stacy said. To be clear, encouraging people to spend more is not Stacy’s typical MO. Having worked with more than 270 clients over 25 years, she said, “I’ve had this conversation of ‘You really need to spend more money’ with maybe three people.” What’s next: We’ll catch up again with Abbey in a few weeks. But next week, you’ll learn more about a surprising turn of events for Mariza and Geffrey Gordon.

cnn.com.title: Roth IRA or 457(b): Which is better for your retirement savings? An expert weighs in
cnn.com.text: Sometimes, the problem with savings is less about where to get the money than which savings vehicle to put them in, since they each have their own advantages and disadvantages. In this week’s Ask the Expert for CNN’s Savings Challenge, Douglas Boneparth, certified financial planner and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, breaks down the differences between a Roth IRA and a 457(b), which is offered to employees of some state and local governments and tax-exempt organizations. A reader from Florida asks: “I am skeptical of the future conditions of the economy and the status of Social Security. Where should I focus first for investing and saving for retirement? Roth or 457(b)? I often hear: do both, balance them out; but I am specifically asking which to maximize first. And if you have an explanation as to why, that would be very helpful.” DOUG: I love this question because you’re not asking whether to save for retirement. You already know you should. You’re asking how to do it smarter. That’s a much better conversation to be having. The 457(b) is an underrated account, especially for public employees. Unlike a 401(k), there’s no 10% early withdrawal penalty, meaning you can tap it before age 59½ without penalty. If early retirement is part of the plan, that matters a lot. Contributions also reduce your taxable income today, which is valuable if you’re in a higher bracket now. However, the Roth is powered by something the 457(b) can’t match: tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals in retirement. You pay taxes now and you never pay taxes on that money again. And here’s where your Social Security concern gets interesting. Roth withdrawals don’t count toward the income thresholds that determine how much of your benefit gets taxed. If benefits shrink or get taxed more aggressively down the road (which is a legitimate concern) having a tax-free income source gives you flexibility a pre-tax account simply can’t. If your 457(b) has an employer match, grab it first. But if you’re forced to prioritize one, go with the Roth. Tax-free income in retirement is one of the most powerful tools available to today’s savers. And given your skepticism about Social Security, you might sleep better at night knowing you had that tax-free bucket to draw from. Have your own savings question for Doug? Please send it to savingschallenge@cnn.com. Tip of the week: Even if you can only save a little, compounding can help … a lot Consistently saving and investing even small amounts of money can grow into an impressive nest egg over time. For example, if you consistently save $200 a month ($2,400 a year) from ages 25 to 65 in a pre-tax account like a 401(k), 403(b) or deductible IRA, you could have a $512,000 nest egg by age 65, according to the Plan Sponsor Council of America. That assumes an average annual return of 7%. If you can only salt away $100 a month ($1,200 a year pre-tax), but your employer offers a dollar-for-dollar match on that amount, you still can end up with half a million dollars after 40 years. And if you’re able to save $200 after-tax in a Roth IRA, you will have half a million dollars tax-free when you retire.

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: Inside Erik Prince’s secretive operation taking on Haiti’s gangs
cnn.com.text: Trees wrap around buildings, roots sprout from riverbeds of plastic trash, and vines creep down the street. Nature is working to reclaim downtown Port-au-Prince after years of dereliction and gang warfare. But at dawn, through this post-apocalyptic urban forest still come streams of humanity: Hundreds of civilians walk through this dead zone every day, some carrying food, others heading to work — as first light permits them to cross gangland and into what’s left of the city’s free streets. It is a scene of desperation that repeats at dusk, when the same single file of hundreds returns home. Here were once waterfront villas, a cathedral, a busy market frequented by tourists. No one comes here anymore — unless they have no other choice. Years of political turmoil, corruption and the ascendance of a deadly gang coalition are suffocating Haiti’s capital city. The US and international community have repeatedly tried and failed to help bring order. Now, the remnants of Haiti’s government have rolled the dice with a very different option: a US private security tycoon. STREAMING NOW: Haitians are scared to venture out of their homes. Here, life is always on the line. Erik Prince says he can help. Upgrade to watch the full report. Erik Prince and his private security teams were contracted by the US government during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, most remembered for Blackwater employees opening fire in Baghdad’s Nusoor Square, killing 17 Iraqi civilians. Four of his contractors were convicted in the US and later pardoned by President Donald Trump. Now he’s in Haiti, where his mercenaries are working with elite local police to break the gangs’ chokehold — a secretive project known as the “Task Force.” Prince has also introduced drone warfare to Haiti, with over 2,000 strikes since the Task Force began its operation last March. One seen by CNN shows a tiny drone flying straight into what looks like a water tank on a roof. It ruptures, and then suddenly the building is aflame — a strike on what a Task Force source said was a gang factory for Molotov cocktails. “Insurgencies are not defeated by taking out just leadership,” Prince said last month, in an exclusive interview with CNN in Port-au-Prince. “I know there’s been obsession of that in the United States, but wars are won by taking significant numbers of enemy manpower off the battlefield.” “They are evil criminals and the best place for them is in the ground.” It’s an approach that critics say defies international law and due process. But for many Haitians exhausted by years of gang atrocities, the more important question is: Is it working? A secretive project Prince’s new company Vectus Global was hired by Haiti’s interim government last year. The Task Force now works in a fractured security landscape that includes the Haitian National Police, the new UN-mandated Gang Suppression Force, Haiti’s long-neglected army and a network of armed vigilante groups. Soft-spoken in person but prolific on social media, Prince touts his work in Haiti as a model to other failing states with their own intractable security problems. “When we started, a police truck was lost every week — attacked, ambushed, burned, the occupants slaughtered, butchered,” Prince said, standing on a rooftop overlooking gang-held parts of the capital. “That’s done now, because there’s much better response, quicker air support, drones, whatever, that prevents the police from being overmatched.” Promised milestones have been elusive. When his contract was announced early last year, Prince said he aimed to free up key roads within a year, making it possible to drive from the northern port city of Cap Haitien to Port-au-Prince. Eighteen months on, the vital route remains strangled by gang checkpoints. International flights to Port-au-Prince are stopped because of the risk of being shot over gang territory. General elections were supposed to be held in December; they have been postponed indefinitely. Nonetheless, the past year has, at the least, halted the gangs’ advance in the capital, according to one assessment. The United Nations, which monitors the situation on the ground with quarterly updates, said in September that security operations “have contributed to halting the expansion of gangs in Port-au-Prince and cleared some areas from gang control, including in downtown.” The death toll remains high. Of the 5,700 people killed or injured in 2026, more than half were casualties around security operations, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said in early October. The gangs are also changing their strategies. They’re accelerating into other parts of the country, including farming communities that feed the nation. Forcible recruitment of children has tripled over the past year — between 30% and 50% of gang members are now minors, UNICEF estimates. When gangs come under attack, they leave their youngest members behind with orders to fight until the end, one police commander told CNN. An operation in Kenscoff In the mists of the steep hills that ring southern Port-au-Prince, CNN saw one Task Force operation where helicopters manned by foreign contractors assaulted gang positions, and drones detonated amid the clatter of gunfire. Earlier this summer, a gang had massacred at least 47 residents and kidnapped dozens more in the town of Kenscoff, on the main southern route out of the capital. It was an apparent attempt to gain leverage over the Task Force, with the gang leader releasing a video threatening to kill hostages if drones hurt his troops. The gang eventually released its hostages but dug into the tiny nearby hamlet of Bois D’Avril, into which Prince’s foreign ex-special forces flew in September, engaging them in an hours-long firefight. Footage obtained by CNN showed the Haitian National Police’s SWAT unit entering the village, machine-gunfire in the background, and the distant thud of explosions. It also provided a rare sighting of some of Prince’s men, chatting with a SWAT officer who says, “I have heard a lot of things about you.” A heavily armed foreign contractor points out to the officer a hillside building as a good security position. “We will be around the next few days to help you out,” he says, in an apparent Australian accent. It was an operation that local residents cheered, rushing in to burn gang barricades after police declared the area clear. But for now, it’s still too dangerous for the area’s residents to return home. Many are now refugees in their own country, adding to the more than 1.5 million people who are internally displaced in Haiti — about a tenth of the national population. “I’ve been left with nothing,” said one Kenscoff refugee, Luckson Alfrezin, from a cramped encampment in the capital, after the gang killed his uncles, cousins and aunts, and livestock. “It’s like being a car with no lights on. You’re living but you don’t see why. You are already dead.” A central question is how Haiti’s patchwork forces will hold and defend reclaimed areas like Kenscoff. It’s a role beyond what Prince’s small force is designed to do, but where coordination with the still-growing Gang Suppression Force and Haitian National Police is evolving. How much is Prince getting paid? Prince would not disclose the annual fee he receives for work with the Task Force, claiming only that it is a “fraction” of the cost of the short-lived Multinational Security Support mission — an initiative backed financially and logistically by the United States, that once envisaged 5,500 foreign police in Port-au-Prince. “Our cost is one-sixth of what their annual camp cost was,” Prince said. The sum is likely in the tens of millions of dollars. His income will be augmented by a deal to help control Haiti’s porous border with the Dominican Republic for the next 10 years in return for 10% of any new customs revenue collected. The long-term contract has raised criticism locally of how Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé is using his mandate as interim leader. Human rights lawyer Rosy Auguste Ducena, who advocates for the rights of victims of violence, says the Haitian public is fed up with the slow pace of change. “Absence and inaction are still the biggest issue with all the security forces operating in Haiti,” she said, pointing out that no major gang leader has been killed in years. So far, the Vectus contractors are perceived as “useless,” she added. “First of all, we don’t notice them, that’s the main thing: We don’t see them. And we know they’re very costly because it’s still our taxes that pay them and  we don’t see the results,” she added, calling for greater accountability from all the security forces operating in the country. Armed groups still operate with “relative impunity” in Haiti, according to Ducena — a fact underlined by dozens of gang social media accounts flaunting their money, weapons, and freedom of movement, in addition to gruesome torture and kidnapping videos. Deadly drone strikes force gangs to pay attention Prince’s drones have had two palpable effects. First, ordinary people have been caught in some of the blasts. The UN counts 85 civilians dead from drone strikes across Haiti, according to a CNN tally of UN reporting, and directly attributes this to a “private military contractor.” Accounting is patchy, however, and rights workers say some deaths may go unreported because of difficulties they have reaching the kinds of gangland areas targeted by drones. The most prominent case was a failed strike on a gang leader’s birthday party in September last year.
